Hi, coaches. It's my pleasure to introduce our next presenter and that is Dr. Liz Odera, all the way from Nigeria, Africa. She's going to present on what makes you unique. I really hope you enjoy this presentation. Over to you, Liz. So the first thing is, what was your initial goal when you started coaching? Your goal may be part of what the organization that you're in has, but you yourself needs to have your own personal goal. So what was your initial goal, even getting to work in that club? And it's very important that you spell it out very clearly in one single sentence. And the goal may not be, I want to just coach tennis. For example, I started coaching because I wanted to change lives through improved health and education. So every one of my lessons included a learning aspect about life and about better health. So I left every single child with something they could go away and do that helped them with what they, how they live their lives. So that I can change the world in my own way. So for you, what is it that makes you wake up each day and say, I'm going to coach today and I'm going to serve people. How? It's very important that in spite of whatever the goal or the mission of the organization that you're in has, personal goals matter because you matter. Okay. So why does all this matter at all? Let's just consider different situations. The first one, situation A. Mary has been asked to take over as the Thursday, take over the Thursday class

as coach and manager. This, since the last coach had already retired and she was managing a class of older folks and she was used to coaching a younger team. However, you're expected in this club to be flexible and be able to fit in. So she joins this group of over 55 Thursday class and she gets to be ignored the whole time. They're just doing their own thing. One of them insists on calling her Sarah, even though she keeps saying, my name is Mary. Usually the team has eight players and this time around one player was unwell and was unable to come and his usual partner was very reluctant to join anybody else. Anyone she partnered him with, he was unhappy and he was even more unhappy when she offered to do so. So that means that there was awkward moments when she had to pair people often and get the doubles going. By the time she ended that lesson, Mary was very upset and she left, she did everything as with the bare minimum that was required and went away. Very sad. And she cried in the bathrooms. That is situation one. And here's the second situation and one of the reasons why we say you cannot serve everybody everywhere all the time. And this is about John. John is a very successful coach. In fact, a lot of people in his area know him and if you come across a good player, you'll show at some stage he had gone through John's hands. So John started off with his own children. He coached them

right from the beginning when they were in junior school and when they moved on to high school, he picked up coaching other children from their former school, the junior school, and the neighborhood that he lived in. And when the numbers grew, he moved from his local court in the neighborhood to public courts about two miles away, which was not too far away. So everybody was able to join him. And while he was doing all that coaching, he also started to take the children to tournaments, which is a normal course of things that happens. So between that and coaching those children and still keeping up with his own children, he then got to be noticed while he was in the public courts by a group of ladies who were getting ready to play league. So they asked him if he could spend some days with them a couple of hours. And he thought he could be able to fit that in between some of the sessions that he was having. And he was pretty successful at that too. He was very popular. So here is John, who reaches a point where he is at his maximum. He is very, very busy. He's making money, but he doesn't have a life. The quality of his life is hard to deal with and he's trying to find time for his family, for himself, a time to relax, a time to take a break. He is not actually earning as much as he would like to, so that he could afford to have support, train some assistants who could also help him. And people would prefer not to be trained

by anybody else. So here is John struggling to balance between what he needs to do for family and he must do for his clients. That is the second situation. Penny and Bob met in high school and they actually played in the tennis team there. And they became friends and after college they got married and took over the running of a private club. And to spark interest in the club and raise revenue they decided to start an annual invitation. And amongst the awards that they were giving was membership for the top four and for the rest of the entries they would be discounted membership offer for the first year. And they got a lot of interest and they continued to run this tournament and build on it. And the best players in the region started to attend training at their club and experience coaches whom they hired specifically to support them. That was primarily to support them so that the name of the club would grow. Unfortunately for them they were not very popular with the coaching, the coaches around the region because those coaches were constantly building and losing players. However they were a very successful club. They managed to raise money, sponsorships, partnerships that they were looking for and many of those juniors who had a history with success in other clubs and other programs under other coaches were now in their under their banner competing in ITF tournaments amongst others.

That is the third situation. And here's my fourth situation. Barry is the name everybody calls. When something is wrong when you need something, when the lights don't come on you look for Barry. When you're not sure where you should be you look for Barry. When you really are looking for an office you look for Barry. When you want to know what time the lights go off you look for Barry. When you want to know how much you should pay you look for Barry. Barry coaches the seven to eighty year olds with the orange ball and they're always very excited and they enjoy their sessions. The swinging sixties who play on Friday evenings absolutely adore Barry and they will not start without him. Barry is the first person who comes in in the morning and the last person to switch off the lights in the evening. Nobody knows when Barry even takes a holiday and then one fine day a letter arrives to everybody's box and when they open it this is what it reads. We regret to inform you of Barry's passing away. Barry passed away while undergoing bypass surgery at 76 years old. He leaves behind his wife and soulmate Marie and their four children and eleven grandchildren. Members confessed that they didn't even know that Barry had a family. Many of them didn't even know what age Barry was. He was just ageless and a lot of people were surprised that Barry was actually ill. That is the fourth situation. So here is the question. What does a coach do and why are you even coaching

The background appears to be an indoor setting with a couch and a framed picture on the wall. The text suggests that this image may be related to a discussion or interview about coaching in sports science.

and why is it so so important to you? I know I keep saying you cannot be everything to everyone and it's true. You can be successful no matter who you serve. You can serve poor people, rich people. You'll still be successful if you choose to be. You can serve young people, old people. You can serve those who are already very well known and performing extremely well. You can serve people on wheelchair right and still be successful. You just need to pick your community. And the question is who is your community? Because when you start to think about that, that is where you begin the first steps to success. What I am giving today is truly just the beginning of being a successful world class coach. First and foremost, you need to be able to spell out why you are coaching and who is the community that you coach. Because it is not about equipment. It's not about facility. At the end of the day, the primary thing is about you and I performing a service to our chosen community. That is what coaching is all about. One of the primary reasons that I really insist on this, clarifying who you serve is very important and why you do what you do. If you don't have a primary reason, you find yourself being taken all over, jumping into all sorts of things and then getting the quality of your life drop. You may be earning more money, but you do not have time. And then there comes the frustrations because

at some point, things don't work the way you want them to. So it's good to know right from beginning, this is who I am. This is who I wish to serve. And this is how I want to serve and I'm ready to attend all the classes, do all the training because I know whom I'm serving and why I'm doing that. So do not try to serve everybody all the time. It doesn't work. Experience shows that it doesn't work. I have been a successful world-class coach. However, my focus was never to coach the best players. It was always to build my community and through building my community, I managed to get to reach hundreds of thousands of young children as well. And it was always about improving health and wellness through tennis. It was always about improving education, giving access to education. And the fact that a large number of those children went on to play tennis around the world and compete to the highest level was a bonus, but it was never the main goal. So it's important that you work out why you want to coach and whom your community is and how you can use tennis to become successful for your community because you are the voice for those whom you serve. So the focus primarily is two things. One, why do you want to coach? Even if you've been a coach for many, many years, it's important that you look at it again and think through what it was like before and why you still want to continue to coach. And two, who really is your community?

And spell it out because if you don't know your community well, you cannot be a changemaker. You cannot provide positive influence for success. Once you understand your community, you can create changes. And believe me, there is nothing like a coach in making successful people. We are builders and will always be builders. We cannot take a step back and let others struggle on their own. And there is space for every single coach at every level to be successful. I gave you four situations. Which one are you? You have choices. There are a lot more situations than those four. This is only the beginning of the courses that I run. And I would love to be able to continue with you, to take you through the different steps you would need to make to spell out your community and even be able to understand why they are so varied even when you just want to work with people within your club. Where there are those who will be with you and those who never seem to understand what it is that you are trying to do and how you can carry all of them forward successfully and still grow as a coach and a leader.
